az_elephant_head.blurb: Elephant Head is a big, seldom-visited formation of more than 1,000 feet on the western side of the Santa Rita Mountains, south of Tucson. Six trad routes go up its north, west and south sides, ranging from an easy third-class scramble to routes in the 5.10 range. Expect an adventurous day: traffic is light, finding the way can be tricky, and rock quality swings from excellent to poor. Descent is usually by the hiker's line down the east side, with long rappels down a western gully as the alternative. There are no facilities, so bring everything you need.
az_elephant_head.parking_note: Take the dirt road toward the south face and leave the car where it becomes too rough to continue; a high-clearance vehicle is strongly advised.

az_pillar_boulder.blurb: Pillar Boulder is a tall, narrow boulder in the Anvil Boulders at the north end of Sedona, a short walk from the creek crossing. It holds six problems, from easy crack lines in the V0 range up to V4, with a pair of V3s between. Two of the harder lines carry a PG13 warning, so tall boulders like this deserve spotters and pads. The Anvil Boulders sit at around 4,300 feet in sandstone, which makes them a useful early-season choice in Arizona's shoulder months.

az_6_knight.blurb: Knight is a sector of the Chessman Area in Bear Canyon on Mount Lemmon, above Tucson. Its six sport lines are on the front face and run from 5.10 to 5.11, with a couple of them standing out as the best on the wall. Around the corner, a handful of trad and mixed lines on the south face are easier but carry R ratings. The front wall stays shaded until about mid-afternoon while the south face gets sun most of the day. The approach is a strenuous scramble up a rocky drainage, roughly a quarter hour.

az_practice_cliff.blurb: Practice Cliff is a small top-rope wall right below the Windy Point overlook on the Catalina Highway, in the Mount Lemmon area near Tucson. It has six short lines, mostly between 5.3 and 5.6 with a couple a notch harder, so it suits beginners, rappelling practice and guided outings. To set anchors you scramble back up and traverse a ledge. Because the overlook sits directly above, expect litter and the occasional dislodged rock from visitors, and bring a rope bag or tarp since broken glass collects at the base.

az_hunchback_pinnacle.blurb: Hunchback Pinnacle is a freestanding formation just below Windy Point on Mount Lemmon, near Tucson. Six routes cover it, mostly bolted lines in the 5.10 to 5.12 range with one easier trad line around 5.7. The hardest-looking line follows the exposed downhill side. It is one of the quickest walks at Windy Point East, about a hundred yards from the highway and under five minutes, which suits a short session. That area is known for the densest concentration of routes on the mountain.

az_big_pine_towers_west_face.blurb: The west face of Big Pine Towers is part of Windy Point East on Mount Lemmon, near Tucson. These short towers have routes on both sides, so you can follow the sun or hide from it. Six climbs here, both bolted and trad, run from 5.8 up to 5.11, with the largest cluster around 5.10. A couple of short, sustained moderates give the otherwise hard towers something for mid-grade climbers. Reaching the base means a drop down a short path and a scree slope below the road.

az_nols_wall.blurb: NOLS Wall is a single-pitch trad wall on the Council Rocks shelf in the West Stronghold of Cochise Stronghold, in southeastern Arizona. Six cracks and corners range from an easy 5.6 through 5.9 to a few 5.10 lines, one of which takes two pitches. The wall is busy with outdoor-school groups running introductory sessions. The walk in is short, roughly fifteen minutes: reach the shelf, follow the trails toward the back of the canyon, then drop into a wash until the cliff appears behind some boulders.
